notes: \cpara{Opens with a thought experiment: sorcery done in public, under skeptical supervision, would make most people, ``I think,'' ``fairly curious.''}
\cpara{Turns it: the sorcerer wants to use the power in public without anyone becoming curious, and asks whether there is a spell that stops curiosity.}
\cpara{The answer: say ``Science!''}

\cpara{Explains why ``Science!'' is empty: it says nothing about how the light will behave or how to make one. The test and the term come from ``Mysterious Answers to Mysterious Questions'' (25 August 2007), where a mysterious answer ``acts as a curiosity-stopper rather than an anticipation-controller.''}

\cpara{Applies the point to an ordinary light bulb. ``Electricity!'' is a password in the sense of ``Guessing the Teacher's Password'' (22 August 2007): it does not let you calculate what to expect. The footnote tells physicists to substitute a problem in evolutionary theory.}
\cpara{Claims that a light bulb you believed to be scientifically inexplicable would take all of your attention.}

\cpara{The post's key step, and it leaves something out. ``Scientifically explicable'' is taken to mean that ``someone else knows how the light bulb works,'' and on hearing it, the post says, ``you don't know more than you knew earlier.'' About how the bulb will behave, that is so. But the phrase also tells the listener that the bulb breaks no known law of nature, and that the answer can be found. A bulb that science could not explain would show that something the listener took as settled is mistaken. That is a reason for it to draw more attention than an explained bulb, and it does not depend on who else knows.}

\cpara{Answers the objection in the form of fame and fortune, and then suggests that what remains is ``spite.'' The charge comes as a question, with no evidence. The reason given in the previous note is neither greed nor spite, and the post does not consider it.}
\cpara{Concedes that for uses such as technology it matters whether someone already knows, and asks why it should matter to one's own curiosity.}

\cpara{The reductio. It works because a hovering green elephant cannot be fitted into anything the reader knows, and a voice saying that someone knows the reason does not change that. A light bulb said to be scientifically explicable does fit. The example shows the difference described in the note on ``scientifically explicable.''}
\cpara{The linked page is a drawing of this scene, posted on a reader's blog on 24 June 2012. The link was added to the post after its 2007 date.}
\cpara{Turns to the author's own ignorance: the ultimate laws of physics, and human anatomy apart from the brain.}
\cpara{Asks whether, for curiosity's sake, the unknown laws of physics should intrigue more than the unknown workings of one's own body.}

\cpara{Asks why a light spell should intrigue the reader more than raising a hand, which the cerebellum, ``among other brain areas,'' coordinates in ways the reader does not understand either. The answer to ``Why should there be a double standard'' is the one in the note on ``scientifically explicable'': the spell would break known physics, and the raised hand does not.}
\cpara{Asks whether the reader knows what they are, and why it should matter to curiosity which parts of the answer science knows.}
\cpara{A list of everyday puzzles.}
\cpara{Concludes: prioritize if you must, but do not complain that science has emptied the world of mystery, since the reader could then be talked into ignoring an elephant.}

\clogic{The reply is that much remains unknown to the reader, so the world still holds puzzles. It says nothing about the things the reader does come to understand. The author took that up later, in ``Joy in the Merely Real'' (20 March 2008), which links back to this post: things are ``allowed to be unmagical, knowable, scientifically explicable, in a word, real, and yet still worth caring about.''}
\cpara{Tells physicists to substitute a problem in evolutionary theory, where the substance of the theory is also in calculations few people can do.}
\cpara{Says the author is not proud of not knowing anatomy, and is unlikely to learn it soon.}
